sentences.text: Kelenken is the largest-known phorusrhacid, estimated to be 10% larger than its largest known relatives.
The holotype skull of Kelenken is 716 mm long, making it the largest known bird skull. This skull is very massive, triangular from above, and compressed from top to bottom at the hind portion.

The holotype consists of a nearly complete skull that is somewhat crushed, preserving most eye sockets, the skull roof, braincase, and left quadrate bone. The occipital table of Kelenken is very wide and low, giving it a rectangular appearance from behind, similar to Devicenzia.
The specimen includes a left tarsometatarsus, a partial foot phalanx, and some indeterminate fragments.
Its skull measures 716 mm in length, holding the record for the largest known bird skull.
This giant bird was approximately 10% larger than previously known large species like Phorusrhacos.

Fossils of a phorusrhacid were discovered around 2004 by Guillermo Aguirre-Zabala about 100 meters from the railroad in Comallo. Kelenken fossils were found in pyroclastic outcrops of the Collón Curá Formation near Comallo in Patagonia.
The specimen was designated the holotype of the new species Kelenken guillermoi in 2007.

Large lacrimal bone expansions above the eyes suggest phorusrhacids hunted by sight in open, sunlit areas rather than shaded forests. The open environment of the time favored large, cursorial animals like Kelenken.

Chiappe and Bertelli argued in 2006 that the discovery of Kelenken challenged the idea that larger phorusrhacids were less agile than smaller ones. Chiappe stated in 2006 that Kelenken could run faster than previously assumed for large phorusrhacids, despite not being as swift as an ostrich.
John J. Flynn commented in 2006 that other large South American predators were less numerous and agile than phorusrhacids, which had ample grazing mammal prey.

Degrange found in a 2020 study that phorusrhacids evolved from a seriema-like ancestor into two main skull morphotypes. The "Terror Bird Skull Type" included Kelenken and other large members and was more specialized with rigid skulls compared to the plesiomorphic "Psilopterine Skull Type". Studies show that both phorusrhacid skull types handled prey similarly, but the rigid "Terror Bird" skulls were adapted for handling larger prey.

Degrange and colleagues conducted a 2010 study using Finite Element Analysis and CT scans to estimate the bite force and stress distribution of the phorusrhacid Andalgalornis. Researchers suggested Andalgalornis either fed on small prey swallowed whole or used an "attack-and-retreat" strategy with repetitive beak strikes for large prey.

Tambussi and colleagues analyzed the neck flexibility of Andalgalornis in a 2012 study, finding its neck divided into three sections. Tambussi and colleagues assumed that the neck adaptations of Andalgalornis for carrying a large head and rising after a strike were also true for other large phorusrhacids.
Bertelli and colleagues classified Kelenken as a member of the family Phorusrhacidae in 2007. Kelenken belongs to the family Phorusrhacidae.
A 2011 phylogenetic analysis found Kelenken and Devincenzia to be sister taxa.
A 2015 analysis found the subfamily Phorusrhacinae to be polyphyletic.
Phorusrhacids are an extinct group within Cariamiformes, whose only living members are seriemas.

Kelenken lived during the Middle Miocene epoch. The age of the sediments containing Kelenken is estimated to be about 15 million years old, corresponding to the middle Miocene. The time range for Kelenken is estimated from 15.5 to 13.8 million years ago.
Kelenken is known from the Collón Curá Formation and lived during the Colloncuran age when open environments predominated.
Kelenken belongs to the subfamily Phorusrhacinae, which includes Devincenzia.
Phorusrhacids were present in South America from the Paleocene until the Pleistocene.
The classification of European fossils assigned to phorusrhacids is disputed.
